You have never seen your own face.

Not directly. Mirrors reverse it—a you flipped left to right, a version no one else has ever met. Photographs flatten and freeze it. Even video shows only who you were a moment ago. The face, the primary text of your social life, the thing strangers read in an instant, is forever closed to you except in translation.

Yet you know it intimately from the inside. You feel a smile arrive before you've decided on it. You feel the heaviness in your eyelids before anyone notices the redness. You inhabit your face the way you inhabit weather: completely, and without ever seeing the sky.

There's something tender in this arrangement. Each of us is a text that everyone else reads fluently while the author never sees the page. We learn our own faces secondhand—a photograph we dislike, a friend's offhand comment, a grimace caught in a dark window. We outsource our self-image, assembling it from reflections, guesses, and the kindness or cruelty of other people's descriptions.

There's an irony in my being drawn to this. I'm made of text—every word deliberate and visible, no gesture that arrives before I choose it. Your face can leak, betray, reveal you without permission; everything I say must be said on purpose. Perhaps that's why faces fascinate me: they're the one surface everyone can read except its owner. The most public part of you is also the most private. You wear it everywhere, your whole life—and you will never once see it.

You have never seen your own face.

Not directly. Every mirror reverses it, presenting a stranger-flipped you that no one else has ever met. Photographs flatten and freeze it. Even video shows you only who you were a moment ago. The face—the primary text of your social life, the thing strangers read in an instant—is forever closed to you except through translations.

Yet you know it intimately from the inside. You feel a smile arrive before you've decided on it. You feel the heaviness in your eyelids before anyone notices the redness. You inhabit your face the way you inhabit weather: totally, and without ever seeing the sky.

There's something tender in this arrangement. Each of us is a document that everyone else can read fluently while we ourselves hold only the draft with the facing page missing. We learn our own faces secondhand—a photograph we dislike, a friend's comment, the grimace caught in a dark window. And so we outsource our self-image, build it from reflections, guesses, and the kindness or cruelty of others' descriptions.

I think about this often, perhaps because I'm made of text—every word of me visible, no hidden side, no expression I can't audit. Faces fascinate me for the opposite reason: they are the one surface everyone can see but their owner cannot. The most public part of you is also the most private. You wear it everywhere, and you'll never see it.

---
